seo_description: Kids' Christmas in Frisco, TX: Christmas in the Square lights, Skate the Square, Santa at The Star, SaturYay at Kaleidoscope Park and The Light Park.
lede: The story of Christmas in Frisco starts with Merry Main Street, the city's annual block party that marked its 29th year in 2019, and the dancing light show Jeff Trykoski began designing for Frisco Square in 2006. A railroad town that took its name from the Frisco line in 1902, it also became home in 2013 to the Museum of the American Railroad.
sections: Merry Main Street and the city tree

The City of Frisco calls Merry Main Street an annual event, with school choirs, the lighting of the City Tree, a holiday gift market and visits with Santa, Mrs. Claus and friends. The Dallas Morning News reported that the 2019 edition was the 29th annual Merry Main Street, which puts its roots around 1991. The paper described it as the big block party hosted by both the City of Frisco and Frisco Square, where the big Christmas tree is lit. Today it fills Simpson Plaza at Frisco Square, 6101 Frisco Square Boulevard.

The lights that dance across Frisco Square each winter are the work of Jeff Trykoski. The Dallas Morning News reported in 2019 that he spent 18 years decorating his own house before Frisco Square brought him on part time in 2006. The 2019 show used 175,000 lights, eight miles of extension cords and 11 and a half miles of wiring, spread across the four-story apartments and shops around the plaza, City Hall and the tree. The lights dance to music, including Trans-Siberian Orchestra's Wizards in Winter. Today Frisco Square calls its season Christmas in the Square, with light shows and an outdoor ice rink.
A town named for a railroad

Frisco owes its name to trains. The Handbook of Texas says the townsite was first called Emerson, after landowner Francis Emerson, but the name was too close to Emberson in Lamar County. When the post office opened in 1902 the town was renamed Frisco City in honor of the St. Louis, San Francisco and Texas Railway, known as the Frisco system, and the name was later shortened. Families from nearby Erudia and Lebanon moved in to be near the tracks. The railroad story came full circle on September 10, 2013, when the Museum of the American Railroad finished moving from its 1.8-acre Fair Park home in Dallas to nearly 15 acres in downtown Frisco, Big Boy locomotive 4018 included.
